title: Momentum-selective graphene spectroscopy of moiré excitons
abstract: Far-field photoluminescence probes only the light-cone corner of an exciton's momentum content, whereas energy transfer to nearby graphene integrates in-plane momenta up to the inverse spacer thickness $1/z$. For a WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterobilayer we build the transition polarization $\bm{P}_n(\qv)$ of each localized moiré exciton from the registry-dependent vector dipole texture and use each $\bm{P}_n$ for both baths. The two baths rank the states differently: the graphene-rate ratios differ from the optical ones, their ordering inverts with spacer thickness, and the distance exponents at $z=10$\,nm spread by more than two units. These ratios are independent of the transition-dipole prefactor. Within the $C_3$-symmetric leading-harmonic model the chiral $p_+$ and $d_-$ states are also dark at normal incidence yet transfer to graphene at rates comparable to the bright ground state. Their graphene rate depends on the sign of the texture phase, a quantity invisible in far-field emission, which we determine from first principles. In a device this prediction requires a splitting, larger than the symmetry-breaking mixing, that protects the chiral partners. Graphene proximity thus acts as a momentum-selective near-field probe of moiré excitons, and we propose its use as a practical spectroscopy.
summary: This work proposes using energy transfer from moiré excitons in TMD heterobilayers into nearby graphene as a momentum-selective spectroscopic tool. Unlike standard far-field measurements, which are limited to zero momentum, the graphene coupling samples the full in-plane momentum content. This technique allows researchers to characterize otherwise 'dark' exciton states and probe fundamental properties of the exciton dipole texture.
main_problem: To develop a momentum-selective spectroscopy technique for moiré excitons, overcoming the limitations of far-field photoluminescence which only probes the light-cone corner.
main_result: Graphene energy transfer acts as a momentum-selective near-field probe, revealing information about dark exciton states and the sign of the dipole texture phase invisible in far-field emission.
method: The authors construct the finite-q transition polarization P_n(q) for localized moiré excitons and compare the resulting decay rates from optical emission versus energy transfer into graphene.
model_or_system: The system is based on moiré superlattices formed by WSe2/MoSe2 heterobilayers, modeled using an exciton center-of-mass Hamiltonian and analyzed in a plane-wave basis.
key_observables: Transition polarization P_n(q), ratio of graphene decay rates ($\Gamma_G$) to optical rates ($\Gamma_\gamma$), and the relative intensity of dark states.
important_parameters: Spacer thickness (z), moiré potential strength (V_0), and the momentum transfer scale (up to 1/z).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the C3-symmetric leading-harmonic model and assumes that a protecting splitting exists in a real device to observe dark state coupling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the momentum windows probed by far-field PL versus graphene transfer, and quantitatively show that states dark in far-field emission have significant coupling rates to graphene.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the limitation of far-field PL, introduces the graphene energy transfer as a superior probe, calculates the transition polarization, and demonstrates how this probe reveals hidden physics like the sign of the dipole texture phase.
why_interesting: The concept of using energy transfer into a metallic bath (graphene) to map out the full momentum distribution of an exciton is a powerful analogy for open quantum system spectroscopy, linking solid-state physics to quantum optics.
